slides.0.title: History: from Rome to the quality revolution
slides.0.subtitle: How a bulk-wine giant turned toward quality
slides.1.title: Antiquity and the Middle Ages
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Greeks and Romans
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Wine With Seth: the ancient Greeks planted vines near Narbonne in the 5th century BC; the Romans expanded viticulture and Narbonne became a trading hub
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Becoming French
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Wikipedia: Languedoc has belonged to France since the 13th century; Roussillon was acquired from Spain in the mid-17th century and remains culturally Catalan
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Canal du Midi
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Opened in 1681, linking the Mediterranean and the Atlantic and giving wine a water route out (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.content: Vines have grown here for over two thousand years, older than many famous French regions.
slides.2.title: Phylloxera and cheap red
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Phylloxera
slides.2.highlights.0.content: From the 1860s (the timeline says 1868) it destroyed vineyards, and replanting favoured high-yield varieties
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Le gros rouge
slides.2.highlights.1.content: From the late 19th century production shifted to mass-market everyday red; Aramon, Alicante Bouschet and Carignan replaced many quality vines (Wikipedia)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Wartime rations
slides.2.highlights.2.content: It supplied the daily wine ration to French soldiers in both World Wars (Wine With Seth)
slides.2.content: Volume became the region's identity, and set up the later crisis.
slides.3.title: Surplus and turning point
slides.3.highlights.0.title: A sea of Carignan
slides.3.highlights.0.content: In the mid-1960s returning Algerian settlers helped make Languedoc "a sea of Carignan vines" (Wine With Seth); Algerian independence in 1962 ended the blending of Algerian wine (Wikipedia)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Europe's wine lake
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Falling demand for cheap red in the 1970s created a surplus, and the region became a leading contributor to Europe's "wine lake" (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Vine-pull schemes
slides.3.highlights.2.content: EU vine-pull schemes in the 1990s roughly halved French Carignan plantings and encouraged Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.content: Surplus forced change: pull out first, then reposition.
slides.4.title: Quality revolution and today
slides.4.highlights.0.title: From the 1980s
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Vines were uprooted, yields cut by more than half and new appellations created (Wine With Seth); total vineyard area has fallen by over 40% since 1975
slides.4.highlights.1.title: AOC Languedoc
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Coteaux du Languedoc was recognised by decree on 24 December 1985; a decree of 30 April 2007 renamed it Languedoc and added zones such as Corbières (Languedoc AOC page)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Occitanie
slides.4.highlights.2.content: In 2016 it merged into the Occitanie super-region (Wine With Seth)
slides.4.content: Today's Languedoc-Roussillon is a case study in moving from volume to quality.
In which century did the Greeks plant vines near Narbonne?
Wine With Seth gives the 5th century BC.
In which year did the Canal du Midi open?
In which year did Algerian independence end the blending of Algerian wine?
After phylloxera, replanting here mainly favoured what?
High-yield varieties, building a bulk-wine reputation.
In which year did a decree rename Coteaux du Languedoc as Languedoc?
What was the result of the EU vine-pull schemes of the 1990s?
A. French Carignan plantings roughly halved
D. The region merged into Bordeaux
Roughly halved, with Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre encouraged.
